description: Metres of fibre wound per metre of beam span
source: Value kept from the earlier sheet ("Stuttgart paper" numbers, original source not traceable). Plausibility check: Duque Estrada et al. 2026, Sci. Rep. 16:8154 (dual-robot CFW flax-timber pavilion): long-span plate = ~3,830 m of total roving over a ~7.5 m span = ~510 m per m of span (a plate, not a beam; width not given). Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving) gives no span or element data.
comments: Metres of ROVING per metre of span, counting every roving. It does not change with the number of rovings wound at the same time: Di Bari and Duque Estrada both define total roving length = length x rovings x passes, so winding 1 roving at a time (our in-line sensing case) instead of 6 (Di Bari) or 12 (Duque Estrada) gives the same 550 m/m and the same beam mass; only the winding TIME changes (see the winding output rate). Range widened from 440-660 to 400-800 m/m because the value depends on the load and design of the beam. Range is between 400-550 because, according to Stuttgart team, optimizing fiber placement can decrease material use by up to 25%.

description: Mass of one metre of fibre (incl. resin)
source: Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 3.1 and Table 5: flax roving TEX 2400 (2.4 g/m) at a fibre mass ratio of 42% (Eq. 3) = 5.7 g of composite per m of roving (2.4 g fibre + 3.3 g resin at 1.18 g/cm3). Hardener and UV additives excluded, resin loss 0. Check: Di Bari Table 7 gives the resin 1.72e-2 kg CO2e per m of roving; divided by ~5.2 kg CO2e/kg (footprint of the partly bio-based resin implied by Duque Estrada et al. 2026, Sci. Rep. 16:8154: 4,220 kg CO2e/t saving = 44.9% below conventional epoxy) this is ~3.3 g resin per m, which equals what FMR 42% gives for 2.4 g of fibre (2.4 x (1/0.42 - 1) = 3.3 g). Table 5's 13.6 g of resin would give only ~1.3 kg CO2e/kg.
comments: Composite mass per metre of ROVING (fibre + resin) = 0.0057 kg/m, so 1 m of span = 550 m x 0.0057 = 3.1 kg. History: original sheet value 0.006 (unsourced, probably this same Eq. 3); v11/v12 used 0.016 (Table 5: 2.4 g + 13.6 g resin); changed back after the back-calculation in the source column showed that Di Bari's impact results use ~3.3 g resin/m, so Table 5's 13.6 g looks like a typo. Caveat: this is an inference using a resin footprint from a different paper, not proven. CONFLICT with the partners' verbal resin dose (10 ml/m = 11.8 g, i.e. ~14.2 g/m in total, inside the max of this range); Tanya prefers Di Bari over the partners' estimate. Best check: weigh a cured 1 m roving or the partners' demonstrator. Min 0.0048 = ~15% lighter (low resin uptake); max 0.016 = Table 5 reading. Hemp assumed to have the same linear density as Di Bari's flax (TEX 2400); the partners did not give a hemp TEX.

description: Share of the production input mass made of this material (virgin); the shares of one stage add up to 100 %
source: Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 4.1: fibre mass ratio (FMR) 42%; lower bound 15% = Table 5 reading (2.4 g fibre / 16 g composite). Check: Di Bari Table 7 gives the resin 1.72e-2 kg CO2e per m of roving; divided by ~5.2 kg CO2e/kg (footprint of the partly bio-based resin implied by Duque Estrada et al. 2026, Sci. Rep. 16:8154: 4,220 kg CO2e/t saving = 44.9% below conventional epoxy) this is ~3.3 g resin per m, which equals what FMR 42% gives for 2.4 g of fibre (2.4 x (1/0.42 - 1) = 3.3 g). Table 5's 13.6 g of resin would give only ~1.3 kg CO2e/kg.
comments: Hemp share = 42%: Di Bari's stated FMR, which their impact results are consistent with (see source). v11/v12 used 15% (Table 5 reading), the original sheet 60%. Hemp replaces Di Bari's flax at the same 2.4 g/m (assumption). Min 15% = Table 5 / partners' resin dose (10 ml/m); max 50% = a little less resin. No coating or extra fillers, as agreed with Tanya.

description: Share of the production input mass made of this material (virgin); the shares of one stage add up to 100 %
source: Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 4.1: FMR 42% means 58% resin by mass (3.3 g per 2.4 g of fibre). Partners: 10 ml/m of non-bio-based resin (= 11.8 g/m) would give ~83%, the upper bound.
comments: Epoxy share = 58% (complement of the hemp share; v11/v12 had 85%). The partners use a non-bio-based epoxy (Di Bari's GreenPoxy 56 is 51% bio-based); only its density (1.18 g/cm3) comes from the paper. The hardener is assumed to be included in the dose (Duque Estrada mix 100:30 by weight; not modelled separately). Check that "Fiber glue (epoxy resin)" on unit_burdens_dataSources is a fossil epoxy. Shares are re-normalised by the model.

description: Weight of the machine used in this step (used to account for machine wear)
source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: the partners' self-made in-line sensing unit, a small (10 x 15 cm) box with a camera and a Raspberry-Pi-class computer; a computer-vision model estimates roving strength from video of the 4-8 mm wide roving passing at ~20 cm/s (partner description; no datasheet, all machine values are Claude's estimates). SCALED-UP machine assumed: an industrial machine-vision camera with an edge computer in an enclosure. Box + camera + board + mount ~1 kg (Claude estimate); scaled-up ~5 kg (assumption).
comments: Was 800 kg (placeholder for the braiding/rope machine). No braiding/rope machine is included: in-line sensing needs one roving at a time, so the roving is not twisted into a rope (Tanya, partner info). The old "Rope production" step is now this sensing step.

description: Electric power the machine draws while running
source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: the partners' self-made in-line sensing unit, a small (10 x 15 cm) box with a camera and a Raspberry-Pi-class computer; a computer-vision model estimates roving strength from video of the 4-8 mm wide roving passing at ~20 cm/s (partner description; no datasheet, all machine values are Claude's estimates). SCALED-UP machine assumed: an industrial machine-vision camera with an edge computer in an enclosure. Raspberry-Pi-class board 3-8 W + camera + LED light = ~5 W (typical board specs, not retrieved); scaled-up ~30 W for an industrial camera + edge computer (assumption).
comments: Was 3 kW. ~5 W is negligible next to the robot (0.67 kW); energy check: 0.005 kW / 4.1 kg/h = 1.2 Wh/kg. Scaled-up 30 W is a guess.

description: Mass of material the machine processes per hour
source: Partners (verbal): roving passes the sensor at ~20 cm/s. 0.2 m/s x 3600 s/h x 0.0057 kg composite per m of roving (Di Bari Sec. 3.1) = 4.1 kg/h; min/max = 0.15-0.25 m/s; scaled-up 0.5 m/s = 10.3 kg/h (assumption: faster camera/processing, still below Di Bari's 1.0 m/s robot speed).
comments: Was 20 kg/h (placeholder), 11.5 kg/h in v11/v12 (based on 0.016 kg/m). The model counts time per kg of PRODUCT (composite) mass for every step, so the sensor gets the same composite-mass rate as the winding step (the sensor itself only sees the ~1.7 kg/h of dry roving). Scaled-up 0.5 m/s is Claude's assumption.

description: Operating hours before the machine is worn out
source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: the partners' self-made in-line sensing unit, a small (10 x 15 cm) box with a camera and a Raspberry-Pi-class computer; a computer-vision model estimates roving strength from video of the 4-8 mm wide roving passing at ~20 cm/s (partner description; no datasheet, all machine values are Claude's estimates). SCALED-UP machine assumed: an industrial machine-vision camera with an edge computer in an enclosure. Consumer single-board computer/camera used ~1,500 h/y for ~7 y = ~10,000 h (Claude estimate); industrial vision system ~25,000 h (assumption).
comments: Was 50,000 h. Low-cost electronics are not built for a mill duty cycle, so 10,000 h; the effect on results is negligible either way (machine is ~1 kg).

source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: the partners' self-made in-line sensing unit, a small (10 x 15 cm) box with a camera and a Raspberry-Pi-class computer; a computer-vision model estimates roving strength from video of the 4-8 mm wide roving passing at ~20 cm/s (partner description; no datasheet, all machine values are Claude's estimates). description: Weight of the machine used in this step (used to account for machine wear)
source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: KUKA KR210-class 6-axis robot arm winding ONE impregnated hemp roving around a frame with sticks, with a hand-sized self-made peristaltic resin pump on the end-effector (impregnation) - partner description and Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving) setup (KUKA KR210, payload <100 kg). SCALED-UP machine assumed: the same robot at higher speed. KUKA KR 210 R2700 weighs 1,111 kg (Exapro used-robot listing) + ~40 kg for end-effector, pump, resin reservoir and controller (Claude estimate). Temporary winding frames are excluded (as in Di Bari). Scaled-up: same robot.
comments: Was 3000 kg (placeholder). Dominated by the robot; the pump (~0.5 kg) is negligible.

description: Electric power the machine draws while running
source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: KUKA KR210-class 6-axis robot arm winding ONE impregnated hemp roving around a frame with sticks, with a hand-sized self-made peristaltic resin pump on the end-effector (impregnation) - partner description and Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving) setup (KUKA KR210, payload <100 kg). SCALED-UP machine assumed: the same robot at higher speed. Di Bari Sec. 3.3: 0.61 kW at 0.041 m/s and 0.85 kW at 1.0 m/s. Linear interpolation to 0.2 m/s = 0.65 kW, + 0.015 kW for the peristaltic pump (Di Bari Table 1: 1.94 Wh/L x ~7 L/h = ~14 W). Scaled-up 0.5 m/s: 0.72 + 0.015 = 0.74 kW.
comments: Was 6 kW. Energy check: 0.67 kW / 0.2 m/s = 3.4e-3 MJ per m of roving, about 4x Di Bari's 0.85e-3 MJ/m, because our robot moves 5x slower (sensor-limited) at almost the same power. Scaled-up 0.74 kW follows from the assumed 0.5 m/s.

description: Mass of material the machine processes per hour
source: 0.2 m/s (partners: speed set by the in-line sensor) x 3600 x 0.0057 kg composite per m of roving (Di Bari Sec. 3.1) = 4.1 kg/h; min/max = 0.15-0.25 m/s; scaled-up 0.5 m/s = 10.3 kg/h (assumption).
comments: Was 4 kg/h (placeholder), 11.5 kg/h in v11/v12. Winding time per metre of span = 550 m / 0.2 m/s = ~46 min, versus ~1.5 min for Di Bari (6 rovings wound together at 1.0 m/s): ~30x longer, of which 6x is one roving instead of six and 5x is the lower speed. Energy check: 0.67 kW / 4.1 kg/h = 0.16 kWh/kg. Scaled-up 0.5 m/s is Claude's assumption.

source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: KUKA KR210-class 6-axis robot arm winding ONE impregnated hemp roving around a frame with sticks, with a hand-sized self-made peristaltic resin pump on the end-effector (impregnation) - partner description and Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving) setup (KUKA KR210, payload <100 kg). SCALED-UP machine assumed: the same robot at higher speed. Robot lifetime 36,000 h from the robot LCA (Robotics 2021) used on lci_raw_biopol.

source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: KUKA KR210-class 6-axis robot arm winding ONE impregnated hemp roving around a frame with sticks, with a hand-sized self-made peristaltic resin pump on the end-effector (impregnation) - partner description and Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving) setup (KUKA KR210, payload <100 kg). source: Assumed new (virgin) machines.
comments: Kept as virgin: the sensing unit, robot and oven are assumed to be bought new (same convention as the other RAW cases).

description: Weight of the machine used in this step (used to account for machine wear)
source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: the curing oven of Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving) (custom oven 7.5 x 2 x 2.4 m = 36 m3; the paper prints 3600 L, which is inconsistent with these dimensions; wall transmittance 0.135 W/m2K, 20 C outside), curing profile 8 h at 80 C (its headline case). SCALED-UP machine assumed: the same oven, fully loaded. ~75 m2 of insulated oven walls at ~25 kg/m2 + steel frame, heaters and vacuum equipment = ~3,000 kg (Claude estimate; no datasheet). Scaled-up: same oven.
comments: New step (the old sheet had no curing step); Di Bari finds curing is ~45% of the manufacturing GWP, so it must be included. Weight is Claude's guess (wall area 2 x (7.5x2 + 7.5x2.4 + 2x2.4) = 75.6 m2).

description: Electric power the machine draws while running
source: Wall heat loss = U x A x dT = 0.135 W/m2K x 75.6 m2 x 60 K = 0.61 kW for 80 C inside and 20 C outside (Claude calculation from Di Bari Table 3); min 0.2 kW = 40 C profile, max 0.8 kW includes some heat-up. Scaled-up: same oven.
comments: Average electric power while curing. It excludes the heat-up and the vacuum term of Di Bari's model (see output rate for how the total is matched to the paper's per-metre value).

description: Mass of material the machine processes per hour
source: Calibrated to Di Bari Table 6: curing 0.91e-2 MJ per m of roving for 8 h at 80 C / 0.0057 kg/m = 1.6 MJ/kg = 0.44 kWh/kg; 0.61 kW / 0.44 kWh/kg = 1.4 kg/h (= ~11 kg or ~1,900 m of roving per 8 h batch). Other profiles: 16 h at 60 C = 0.75e-2 MJ/m gives 1.7 kg/h; 24 h at 40 C = 0.45e-2 MJ/m gives 2.8 kg/h (max). Min 0.5 kg/h = oven only one third full. Scaled-up: same (Di Bari assume a full oven).
comments: Was 3.9 kg/h in v11/v12 (based on 0.016 kg/m; the per-kg energy is higher for the lighter 5.7 g/m roving). Curing profile follows the paper (8 h at 80 C, Tanya: "according to the paper"). Di Bari's per-metre value assumes the oven is full; a 1 m demonstrator (~3 kg) fills a tiny fraction of a 36 m3 oven, so the true prototype energy per kg is higher (covered by the min). Energy check: 0.61 kW / 1.4 kg/h = 0.44 kWh/kg. Prototype and scaled-up are identical because the paper's value already assumes full loading; a low-temperature profile (24 h at 40 C) would halve it.

description: Operating hours before the machine is worn out
source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: the curing oven of Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving) (custom oven 7.5 x 2 x 2.4 m = 36 m3; the paper prints 3600 L, which is inconsistent with these dimensions; wall transmittance 0.135 W/m2K, 20 C outside), curing profile 8 h at 80 C (its headline case). SCALED-UP machine assumed: the same oven, fully loaded. 8 h batches x ~250 batches/y x ~15 y = ~30,000 h (Claude estimate).
comments: Oven cycles are long (8-24 h) but only a few per week in a lab; same lifetime assumed for scaled-up.

description: Share of the material entering this step that leaves it as usable output (the rest is waste)
source: PROTOTYPE machinery assumed: the curing oven of Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving) (custom oven 7.5 x 2 x 2.4 m = 36 m3; the paper prints 3600 L, which is inconsistent with these dimensions; wall transmittance 0.135 W/m2K, 20 C outside), curing profile 8 h at 80 C (its headline case). SCALED-UP machine assumed: the same oven, fully loaded. Curing does not remove material (Di Bari assume no loss); min 98% allows for trimming of cured overhang (assumption).
comments: Curing is a hold step; the hardened composite stays in the product.

description: Whether the machine is new (virgin) or reused/recycled (recycled)
source: Assumed new (virgin) machines.
comments: Kept as virgin: the sensing unit, robot and oven are assumed to be bought new (same convention as the other RAW cases).

description: Years the product lasts before any repair
source: Design working life of building structures = 50 y (EN 1990, category 4; general knowledge, not re-checked). Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving): functional unit is a structural element in INDOOR applications. Durability of flax-FRP: 12% strength and 19% modulus loss after 12 wet-dry cycles (Queen's University study on durability of natural-fibre-reinforced polymer composites, abstract only).
comments: Kept 50 y (was 50, range 40-60), min widened to 30 y because natural-fibre composites lose strength when moisture cycles (epoxy hydrolysis, fibre-resin delamination). Indoor, dry use assumed. No CFW-specific service-life data exists (Di Bari: results valid for the lab scale, service life not relevant to A1-A3). Claude's judgement. No repair is modelled for this case (repair rows removed: no literature on repairing coreless-filament-wound elements was found; Di Bari 2026 and Duque Estrada 2026 discuss disassembly, reuse and recycling only), so a product that lasts less than the 50 y reference service life is simply replaced (its burdens are scaled by 50/L).

description: Share of the product's end-of-life mass that goes to this route (the routes add up to 100 %): composted
source: Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 5.1-5.2 (end-of-life routes: incineration with energy recovery default; mechanical and chemical recycling; landfill). No EU-wide split for composite waste was found; shares are Claude's estimates anchored on this paper.
comments: Not composted: ~85% of the mass is thermoset epoxy, which is not compostable, and the cured fibre is bonded into it.

description: Share of the product's end-of-life mass that goes to this route (the routes add up to 100 %): recycled (open loop)
source: Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 5.1-5.2 (end-of-life routes: incineration with energy recovery default; mechanical and chemical recycling; landfill). No EU-wide split for composite waste was found; shares are Claude's estimates anchored on this paper.
comments: Typical 5%: mechanical grinding or cement-kiln co-processing of thermoset composites exists but is rare (Claude estimate; no EU split found). Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 5.2: mechanical recycling has a similar total impact to incineration/landfill and "recycling techniques have yet to become a widespread practice". Scaled-up 15%: more recycling capacity (assumption; note methods.md says the scaled-up EoL may not be read by the model).

description: Share of the product's end-of-life mass that goes to this route (the routes add up to 100 %): recycled (closed loop)
source: Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 5.1-5.2 (end-of-life routes: incineration with energy recovery default; mechanical and chemical recycling; landfill). No EU-wide split for composite waste was found; shares are Claude's estimates anchored on this paper.
comments: 0%: no fibre-to-fibre recycling of cured natural-fibre epoxy exists; chemical recycling (pyrolysis, solvolysis) is still at research stage (Di Bari Sec. 5.1). Pyrolysis even raises total GWP by 4.5% versus incineration (Di Bari Table 12).

description: Share of the product's end-of-life mass that goes to this route (the routes add up to 100 %): incinerated with energy recovery
source: Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 5.1-5.2 (end-of-life routes: incineration with energy recovery default; mechanical and chemical recycling; landfill). No EU-wide split for composite waste was found; shares are Claude's estimates anchored on this paper.
comments: Di Bari Sec. 5.2 uses incineration with energy recovery as the DEFAULT end of life for the flax/epoxy CFW element (Ökobaudat Germany). In the Netherlands landfilling combustible waste is banned (general knowledge, not re-checked), so incineration dominates. Typical 85% is Claude's judgement; scaled-up 80% as some material goes to recycling instead.

description: Share of the product's end-of-life mass that goes to this route (the routes add up to 100 %): landfilled
source: Di Bari et al. 2026, "Unveiling the Environmental Impacts of Coreless Filament Winding" (LCA of a flax/epoxy CFW roving), Sec. 5.1-5.2 (end-of-life routes: incineration with energy recovery default; mechanical and chemical recycling; landfill). No EU-wide split for composite waste was found; shares are Claude's estimates anchored on this paper.
comments: Residual landfill (Di Bari route with the lowest C3-C4 GWP, -99% vs incineration). Typical 10% is Claude's judgement (no EU composite-waste split found); scaled-up 5% (landfill diversion targets). Shares add up to 100% (typical 0+5+0+85+10; scaled-up 0+15+0+80+5).
